Career
Senator Gene Yaw was elected to represent the 23rd Senatorial District in Bradford, Lycoming, Sullivan, Tioga, and Union Counties in November 2008.
Prior to running for the Senate, Yaw served as Lycoming County solicitor for 17 years and was named County Solicitor of the Year in 2004. He has also served as general counsel to the Pennsylvania College of Technology for more than 20 years. In 2013, he was elected Chairman of the Pennsylvania College of Technology Board of Directors.
Senator Yaw serves as Chairman of the Environmental Resources and Energy Committee. He is also Vice Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, and a member of the Agriculture & Rural Affairs, Banking & Insurance, Community, Economic & Recreational Development, Rules & Executive Nominations, and the Majority Policy Committees.
Senator Yaw serves on a number of Boards and Commissions including as Chairman of the Center for Rural Pennsylvania, a member of the Chesapeake Bay Commission, a member of the Environmental Quality Board, a member of the Pennsylvania Aggregate Advisory Board, and a member of the Pennsylvania Energy Development Authority.
Senator Yaw is a member of the Lycoming Law Association and Pennsylvania Bar Association, Pennsylvania Association for Justice, and a former member of the Board of Directors of Susquehanna Legal Services. He serves as “Of Counsel” with the McCormick Law Firm in Williamsport, a prominent firm which has been in continuous existence for 150 years.
A U.S. Army veteran, Yaw enlisted and went on to graduate from the United States Artillery and Missile Officer Candidate School in Fort Sill, Oklahoma. He served an overseas tour of duty as an artillery officer and was honorably discharged as a 1st Lieutenant.
He graduated from Montoursville High School, attended Bucknell University, and earned degrees from Lycoming College and the American University School of Law in Washington, D.C.
Senator Yaw has coached Little League Baseball and coached and refereed for the American Youth Soccer Organization. He is a member of the National Rifle Association, Ducks Unlimited, the Nittany Lion Club, and the Williamsport-Lycoming Chamber of Commerce. He received the 2010 Distinguished Citizen of the Year Award from the Susquehanna Council, Boy Scouts of America, the 2011 Lycoming College Alumni of the Year Award, the 2011 CAPPA Community Partner Award, the Central Pennsylvania State of Israel Bonds 2012 Israel Unity Award, the 2013 Pennsylvania Winery Association Industry Supporter Award, the 2014 Pennsylvania College of Technology Centennial Leadership Award, the 2015 Pennsylvania Office of Rural Health Legislator of the Year Award,  the 2019 Pennsylvania Water Environment Association Public Official of the Year Award and the 2021 Pennsylvania Association of Conservation Districts Legislator Leadership Award.
Most recently, Senator Yaw received the 2023 WVIA Good Neighbor Award, the 2023 Marcellus Shale Coalition Shale Gas Advocate Award, and was selected as the 2023 Clean Water Champion by the Choose Clean Water Coalition. Yaw has also been recognized by the National Federation of Independent Business as a Guardian of Small Business for several legislative sessions and by Americans for Prosperity – Pennsylvania for his consistent conservative legislative voting record. In May 2023, Sen. Yaw was named to the City and State Pennsylvania 2023 Energy and Environment Power 100 list.
A Loyalsock Township resident, Yaw is married to Ann S. Pepperman, Esquire. Together they have two children, Scott and Mackenzie, and four grandchildren.

title: Energy and Grid Reliability
raw_text:
Energy and Grid Reliability
WHAT’S THE PROBLEM?
PJM manages the electric grid serving 13 states and the District of Columbia, ensuring power flows from generators to local utilities and ultimately to homes and businesses. As coal and nuclear plants retire, PJM warns new generation is not being added fast enough to meet growing demand.
If this trend continues, consumers could face higher electricity costs, reliability concerns and power shortages.
WHY IS THIS HAPPENING?
A combination of factors has created this problem. Aggressive clean-energy mandates and policies have accelerated the closure of reliable coal and natural gas power plants before adequate replacement generation is available.
At the same time, many neighboring states are retiring their own dispatchable power sources and increasingly relying on Pennsylvania’s energy production to meet demand.
The result is a growing imbalance between electricity supply and demand. Without policies that support reliable, around-the-clock power generation, consumers will face higher costs and a less dependable electric grid.
WHY PA MATTERS
Pennsylvania isn’t just powering itself – we’re helping power much of the eastern United States.
Pennsylvania is the nation’s leading exporter of electricity, producing more power than we consume and sending the excess to neighboring states through the PJM grid. When other states retire reliable power plants or can’t generate enough electricity,
they depend on US to fill the gap.
Without PA and power producing states like West Virginia and Ohio, states like Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey would be
left in the dark.
ARE WE PAYING THE PRICE?
YES!
Pennsylvanians are frustrated by rising electricity bills, and rightfully so. You see, these states don’t exist in a vacuum, and their policy decisions cause a ripple effect throughout the regional grid.
The result is higher costs for families, seniors and businesses.
Pennsylvanians are paying more for electricity even as our state remains the nation’s leading exporter of energy.
THE BLAME GAME
For years, former Gov. Tom Wolf and current Gov. Josh Shapiro pushed to bring Pennsylvania into the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI), an effort that would have imposed new costs on power generation in the state onto consumers. Thanks to Senate Republicans, that proposal was ultimately blocked in court and formally withdrawn last year.
Unfortunately, that prolonged policy fight created years of uncertainty for the energy sector. During that time, investment in new generation stalled, and Pennsylvania saw no new power plants build since 2019, while some existing facilities retired.
The result was predictable: reduced supply, increased demand and higher prices. This is Economics 101.
This problem was intensified when the governor filed a formal complaint with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). His complaint resulted in a settlement that capped rates for all PJM member states and triggered an increase for Pennsylvania ratepayers, all while reducing costs for exporting states like Virginia and Maryland.
Recently, the governor pointed to PJM as the cause of these increases, suggesting the grid operator is driving up costs.
That simply doesn’t match reality.
PJM does not generate electricity or set energy policy. Like an air traffic controller, it simply manages the system based on conditions created by state-level decisions.
THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH
The bottom line is that these rising costs are the predictable result of policies that restrict reliable energy development, discouraged investment and accelerated plant retirements. Now, the governor is trying to redirect blame on the very system that is trying to keep the lights on.
Blaming PJM may be convenient politics, but it ignores years of decision that created the imbalance in the first place.
WHERE DO WE GO FROM HERE?
Despite its century of reliable operation, PJM is now being criticized for struggling to fit intermittent energy into a system designed for constant, stable electricity delivery.
Some have even suggested Pennsylvania should leave PJM altogether. That idea is extraordinarily expensive. Early estimates indicate withdrawing from PJM would cost ratepayers more than $2 billion.
If Pennsylvania is serious about stabilizing electric rates, the solution is not to restructure PJM or walk away from it. The solution is to increase supply. Without building reliable baseload generation, no amount of regulatory reshuffling will bring prices down.
If we want affordable, reliable electricity, we must focus on increasing supply, not searching for scapegoats. Only then can we protect ratepayers and maintain the dependable energy system Pennsylvanians expect and deserve. We need to stop pontificating and start building new dispatchable generation, yesterday.
The Senate is already working on solutions by identifying sites for new power projects, improving demand forecasting and continuing to streamline permitting so plants can actually get built.

title: Monday Rifle Opener
raw_text:
Restoring Monday Rifle Opener
Restoring Pennsylvania’s Traditional Monday Rifle Opener
Protecting Tradition and Supporting Local Economies
For more than 50 years, the first Monday after Thanksgiving served as the traditional opening day of statewide firearms deer season, drawing families, friends and sportsmen from every corner of the state into our forests and towns.
But that tradition was upended in 2019 when the Pennsylvania Game Commission moved the opener to the Saturday after Thanksgiving, a decision that has had unintended and harmful consequences for local economies.
That’s why I’ve introduced
Senate Bill 1244
to restore the traditional opening day and revitalize the economic engine that this annual event once provided.
WHY SENATE BILL 1244?
Pennsylvania’s firearms deer season brings millions of dollars into local economies each year.
Many businesses have shared with me that the traditional Monday opener created several days of sustained customer activity that helped support their annual revenue.
The opening day of rifle season has long been one of the busiest weekends of the year for small businesses like:
Hotels and Motels
Restaurants and Diners
Bars and Taverns
Sporting Goods Retailers
Convenience Stores and Gas Stations
Local Outfitters
Moving the opener to Saturday spread activity differently and reduced many of the long-standing economic benefits that communities had relied upon for decades.
With hunters heading into the woods earlier and having less time after the holiday to prepare, there are fewer overnight stays, fewer meals eaten in local restaurants and less participation in community fundraisers that relied on traditional timing.
One volunteer fire company in my own district saw turnout at its annual fundraiser plummet from hundreds to just a few dozen last year.
WHAT SENATE BILL 1244 DOES NOT DO
Let me be clear:
Senate Bill 1244 is not about wildlife management or interfering with the Game Commission’s authority to regulate deer populations.
The Game Commission plays a critical role in managing our wildlife resources, and nothing in this proposal changes that. This effort is focused solely on the economic impact in communities like those in my district that rely on the traditional structure of rifle season.
WHAT’S THE STATUS?
Senate Bill 1244 was introduced on March 23, 2026, and continues to receive strong support from hunters and sportsmen across the Commonwealth.
Unfortunately, progress has been slowed due to continued opposition from the Game Commission and resistance from a few legislators.
Despite widespread support among many hunters, local businesses and a bipartisan group of legislators, this opposition has prevented the bill from advancing as quickly as supporters would like.
SO, NOW WHAT?
Stay engaged.
Contact your senators and representatives, tell them why it’s important to you to see the opening day of rifle season restored to the Monday after Thanksgiving and ask them to support Senate Bill 1244.
You can find and contact them directly on the General Assembly’s ‘Find my Legislator’ webpage.
OR you can easily
fill out this form on my website
voicing your support, and I will personally pass your message along.
Your voice has helped keep this issue alive, and continued support will be critical as we work to move Senate Bill 1244 forward. Keep talking about it, keep sharing your story, and together we can restore a tradition that has served Pennsylvania well for generations.

title: Yaw Bill to Formalize End-of-Life Care Decisions Approved by House Committee
raw_text:
Yaw Bill to Formalize End-of-Life Care Decisions Approved by House Committee
Posted on
October 8, 2026
October 8, 2026
HARRISBURG – Legislation to formally recognize Pennsylvania Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST) and establish a clear legal framework for their use across all health care settings was approved today by the Health Committee in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, according to Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23), sponsor of
Senate Bill 730
.
POLST is a medical order, completed after a conversation between a patient and a health care professional, that spells out the specific treatments a seriously ill patient does or does not want in an emergency or at the end of life. Unlike general planning documents, POLST is designed for individuals with serious or advanced illness whose medical decisions may need to be followed immediately by doctors, nurses and emergency personnel.
“The use of a POLST gives patients more control over their care by turning their wishes into clear medical orders that providers can act on right away,” Yaw said. “It helps ensure that patients, their families and their physicians are all on the same page when critical decisions have to be made.”
Under current practices, POLST forms are not consistently recognized or applied across all care settings in Pennsylvania. Senate Bill 730 addresses that gap by providing statutory authority so that POLST forms are honored statewide by health care providers and emergency medical services.
Yaw noted POLST is different from an advance directive. Advance directives generally identify a surrogate decision-maker or provide broad guidance about future care preferences, often in situations that are not yet foreseeable. POLST translates a patient’s current medical condition and treatment preferences into a physician -or clinician-signed medical order that must be followed immediately, ensuring care aligns with the patient’s wishes in real time.
“The Pennsylvania Medical Society (PAMED) is pleased to support Senate Bill 730, legislation that will establish a standardized and enforceable framework for end-of-life healthcare decisions,” said Arvind Cavale, MD, president of PAMED. “Authorizing POLST forms will help ensure that a patient’s care aligns with their wishes regarding life-sustaining treatments in emergencies. These forms will create a standard of care across all care settings and will provide much-needed peace of mind to patients and give healthcare professionals clear guidelines for care. Statutorily authorizing POLST forms will allow patients to make their end-of-life decisions clear to all healthcare professionals. PAMED applauds Sen. Yaw for his leadership on this issue and is happy to support this effort.”
Yaw said the legislation is also supported by the Pennsylvania Homecare Association, Pennsylvania Academy of Family Physicians, the Pennsylvania Association of Elder Law Attorneys and others.
The bill now moves to the full House of Representatives for consideration.

title: Yaw, Miller Bill Limiting Use of PFAS in Firefighting Foam Approved by Senate
raw_text:
Yaw, Miller Bill Limiting Use of PFAS in Firefighting Foam Approved by Senate
Posted on
October 5, 2026
HARRISBURG – A bill to limit the use of firefighting foam containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) was approved by the state Senate today, according to Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23) and Sen. Nick Miller (D-14), sponsors of the measure.
Senate Bill 980
would restrict the manufacture, sale, distribution and use of firefighting foam containing PFAS beginning in 2027. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, PFAS are man-made chemicals used since the 1940s that can accumulate in the environment and the human body over time, with studies linking exposure to adverse health effects.
“Compared to other emergency responders, firefighters can face significantly higher levels of PFAS exposure, putting them on the front lines of this national public health challenge,” Yaw said. “This bill is a commonsense response which has already been adopted by many states. It will undoubtedly protect firefighters moving forward, while also safeguarding our ground and surface water from contamination.”
“This bipartisan legislation takes decisive action to phase out dangerous substances, protecting the long-term health of our frontline heroes while preventing lasting contamination of our soil and water,” said Miller. “It reflects our responsibility to those who risk their lives in service to our communities. I look forward to advancing this bill as we put the well-being of those who serve at the forefront, safeguard public health and advocate for environmental protection.”
The lawmakers said the bill reflects years of collaboration with fire service leaders, emergency responders and industry representatives since its introduction in 2019. The proposal would allow fire companies to use Fire Company and Emergency Medical Services Grant funding to cover the cost of properly disposing of PFAS-containing foam. The state fire commissioner, working with the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, would oversee safe and environmentally responsible disposal.
The bill includes an exemption for facilities where PFAS-based foam remains necessary for safety, such as airports, chemical plants, oil refineries and sites handling flammable liquids or natural gas.
Senate Bill 980 now moves to the House of Representatives for consideration.

title: Yaw Urges PJM to Focus on Generation Growth, Grid Reliability
raw_text:
Yaw Urges PJM to Focus on Generation Growth, Grid Reliability
Posted on
October 1, 2026
HARRISBURG – In a
letter
to the PJM Interconnection Board of Managers, Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23), chair of the Senate Environmental Resources and Energy Committee, urged the regional transmission organization to resolve governance issues and refocus its attention on the growing need for new generation, transmission and reliable, affordable power.
“Pennsylvania is ready, willing and able to support the generation growth necessary to power our economic future,” Yaw said. “PJM needs to focus its resources on clearing the generation queue, integrating new large loads, restoring market price signals and building the transmission infrastructure needed to support new growth. We cannot afford to lose sight of the real challenge: making sure there is enough power to keep up with demand.”
Yaw noted that rapid load growth, driven in large part by the expansion of data centers without their own power supply, is occurring as reserve margins shrink and regulatory constraints continue to create challenges for the PJM system.
The PJM region serves approximately 67 million people across 13 states and the District of Columbia. Pennsylvania has long been a major energy supplier to the region, exporting reliable, dispatchable power while maintaining critical infrastructure needed to keep the lights on.
In his letter, Yaw expressed concerns over Gov. Josh Shapiro’s position on the Federal Power Act Section 205 filing rights, which could lead to costly litigation and divert attention and resources from the more pressing need to increase generation capacity. Yaw wrote that diverting time and capital into litigating an unworkable governance mandate will not build a single megawatt of capacity.
More than 200 gigawatts of generation capacity currently sit in the PJM queue, with over 20% of that capacity located in Pennsylvania. Yaw said the challenge is not a shortage of generation projects, but a lack of regulatory and market clarity needed to move those projects forward.
Yaw also pointed to governance reforms that have already achieved broad consensus through negotiation and compromise, including changes involving the PJM Board Nominating Committee, Board structure and stakeholder process. He urged PJM to move forward with those agreed-upon reforms rather than becoming mired in prolonged litigation.

September 30, 2026

title: Yaw Issues Statement on EPA Repeal of Biden Power Plant Rule
raw_text:
Yaw Issues Statement on EPA Repeal of Biden Power Plant Rule
Posted on
September 16, 2026
HARRISBURG – State Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23), chairman of the Senate Environmental Resources and Energy Committee, issued the following statement after the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) this week
repealed
the Biden administration’s 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants and proposed a related action under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act:
“In April 2024, I warned that Washington’s so-called Clean Power Plan 2.0 would force premature retirements of coal and natural gas generation, drive up rates and put the PJM grid in a worse position than it was already in. That is exactly what the rule was built to do.
“The EPA has now acknowledged the requirements it imposed were not proven to work and could have forced power plants to shut down rather than meet standards they could realistically achieve. The federal mandate, hanging over every coal unit and every new gas plant, told capital to stay home. You cannot ask a company to put billions of dollars into a plant with a 30-year life and then reserve the right to outlaw it.
“The result is the mess our committee has been documenting all year. Demand is rising because of data centers, manufacturing and ordinary household use. Dispatchable generation is not keeping up. PJM has been sounding the alarm. Ratepayers are already paying for scarcity. Neighboring states that retired plants and joined carbon compacts have been happy to lean on Pennsylvania when the wind dies. That is not an environmental program. That is cost shifting.
“Repealing the 2024 rule removes a $310 billion federal threat and gives operators a chance to keep running the units that actually show up and produce power no matter the weather.
“Pennsylvania’s job does not change with a press conference in Houston. We still have to permit plants, pause any expansion of renewable mandates and insist that PJM assign costs to the states whose policies created the shortage. Pennsylvania families should not be asked to sit in the dark so someone else’s climate timeline can be met on paper.
“I call on Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation to defend this repeal and the Section 111 finding, and I call on the Shapiro Administration to stop treating reliable generation as a problem to be managed away. The demand is here. The fuel is here. The only missing piece has been permission to build.”

raw_text:
Owlett, Pickett, Yaw Announce State Grants for Tioga, Bradford County Projects
Posted on
September 15, 2026
HARRISBURG
– Reps. Clint Owlett (R-68) and Tina Pickett (R-110) and Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23) today announced more than $2.3 million in Local Share Account (LSA) grants have been approved by the Commonwealth Financing Authority (CFA) to support water and wastewater infrastructure, road maintenance, public safety and emergency preparedness projects in Tioga and Bradford counties.
Local Share Account grants are funded through gaming revenues under Act 71 of 2004 and support economic development, community improvements and projects that enhance the quality of life for Pennsylvania residents.
“These investments will help communities address needs that are essential to the safety and well-being of their residents,” said Owlett. “Reliable water and wastewater systems, safe roads, dependable municipal equipment and strong emergency services are things people count on every day. This funding will help our local communities make necessary improvements, replace aging equipment and be better prepared when emergencies arise.”
“These investments fulfill a critical funding need for our municipalities and support community projects that residents of Bradford County, and the entire Northern Tier, want to see,” Pickett said. “I am pleased Rep. Owlett, Sen. Yaw and I were able to back these investments and I applaud our municipal leaders for their consistent efforts to strengthen our region.”
“These investments address some very practical needs in our communities,” Yaw said. “Replacing aging wastewater infrastructure, improving road maintenance, providing police and public works crews with the equipment they need and protecting an important historic property will strengthen local services and help ensure these assets serve residents for years to come. I was pleased to join Rep. Owlett and Rep. Pickett in supporting these projects.”
“This project is critical to protecting the Troy Sale Barn and ensuring this historic community gathering place can continue serving the region for another 100 years,” said the Troy Sale Barn Board of Directors. “The partnership between the Troy Sale Barn Operating Corporation, the Troy Municipal Authority and numerous community partners have been essential to preserving and maintaining the barn. This strategic investment would not have been possible without the support of our elected officials. We are incredibly grateful to Sen. Yaw and Rep. Owlett for their continued support of the Troy Sale Barn and their commitment to strengthening our communities.”
“On behalf of the Tioga County Board of Commissioners, we want to thank Sen. Yaw and Rep. Owlett for their continued support of Tioga County and their advocacy for these important projects,” said Marc Rice, Tioga County commissioner. “These LSA awards represent meaningful investments in our communities, supporting critical public infrastructure, law enforcement, and the needs of our local municipalities. We are grateful to see these much-needed resources invested here in Tioga County and appreciate the strong partnership we have with our state legislators as we continue working together to move these important projects forward.”
“These funding awards will have a meaningful and lasting impact by supporting critical infrastructure improvements, police vehicle purchases and truck purchases,” said Daryl Miller, Doug McLinko and Zachary Gates, Bradford County commissioners. “Local governments often face significant financial constraints, and the leadership and advocacy shown by Reps. Owlett and Pickett to help ensure our municipalities have the resources needed to serve residents effectively and responsibly. We are grateful for your continued commitment to rural communities and for working collaboratively to bring these grants to our county.”
The approved projects include:
•
Athens Borough – $67,150
to purchase a new police interceptor vehicle to replace an existing decade-old patrol vehicle that has persistent and expensive mechanical issues. The project includes the purchase of a vehicle, upfitting and custom graphics.
•
Central Bradford Progress Authority, on behalf of Troy Municipal Authority and Troy Sale Barn Operating Corporation – $465,986
to replace a deteriorated retaining wall behind the historic Troy Sale Barn in Troy Borough. The project includes demolition of the failed dry-laid fieldstone wall, construction of a new reinforced concrete retaining wall, drainage improvements and site restoration. LSA funds will be used for construction, engineering and administrative costs.
•
Columbia Township – $125,370
to purchase and upfit a new utility truck to replace an aging 2016 maintenance vehicle that has experienced significant rust, frequent breakdowns and approximately $18,000 in repairs over the past three years. The new truck will improve public works operations and allow the township to clear roads more efficiently during snow events and severe weather. LSA funds will be used for vehicle purchase and upfit costs.
•
Lawrenceville Borough – $385,025
to make electrical improvements at the municipal water treatment plant. The project will replace and relocate electrical components that have been damaged by chlorine and moisture exposure, improving the reliability of the treatment facility. LSA funds will be used for construction, engineering and administrative costs.
•
Liberty Area Municipal Authority – $218,700
to make improvements at the wastewater treatment plant, including new sand media, distribution piping and a chemical mixer system. The upgrades will improve treatment operations and help the facility remain in compliance with permitting and regulatory standards. LSA funds will be used for construction, engineering and administrative costs.
•
Mansfield Borough – $56,375
to purchase a new marked police patrol vehicle equipped with police equipment. The vehicle will strengthen the borough’s limited patrol fleet, improve response times and enhance officer and community safety. LSA funds will be used for vehicle purchase.
•
Rome Township – $335,043
for the reclamation and reconstruction of Robinson Road from North Rome Road to the top of the hill. Funding will support the full-depth reclamation of existing sealcoat surface to reuse the existing materials as part of the new road structure. Following reclamation, an additional subbase layer will be added and new sealcoat will be applied.
•
Tioga County – $250,000
to improve water security in Nelson Township by adding a backup water well, relocating water intake controls, replacing aging valves and installing greensand filtration systems. The improvements will provide a more reliable source of potable water and strengthen the county’s ability to maintain service during emergencies and severe weather. LSA funds will be used for construction, engineering and administrative costs.
•
Towanda Borough – $44,030
for the purchase of a specialized manhole repair and removal tool to improve the efficiency, safety and quality of municipal infrastructure maintenance operations. The purchase of this equipment will help prevent injuries, delays and improper repairs which can lead to water intrusion, road damage and public safety concerns.
•
Ward Township, on behalf of the Blossburg Volunteer Fire Department – $176,003
to purchase new mobile and portable radios. The new digital, P-25-compliant equipment will replace outdated radios that are increasingly difficult and costly to repair, improving communications and reliability for emergency responders.
•
West Burlington Township – $28,200
to purchase and install two emergency generators, one at the municipal building and one at the township garage. The generators will maintain essential township operations and provide emergency power to facilities that serve as warming shelters during power outages and severe weather.
•
Windham Township – $200,000
to purchase a new 4WD heavy-duty truck with a plow to be used for the maintenance of the streets and roads. The vehicle will replace the existing 20 year-old truck. It will also be used to haul stone materials to project areas.

“These investments address two important needs in Sullivan County: improving critical infrastructure and maintaining access to quality healthcare,” Yaw said. “Upgrading Davidson Township’s wastewater facility will help it better withstand future flooding, while improvements to the Sullivan County Medical Center will provide a safer, more comfortable environment for patients and staff. Funding will be used to replace the medical center’s failing multizone HVAC system with a modern, energy-efficient VAV system to address unreliable temperature control, high humidity and poor indoor air quality. Yaw and his team in helping us continue investing in healthcare access here in Sullivan County.”

Yaw, Flick: Nearly $650,000 Awarded to Lycoming, Union County Projects

HARRISBURG – State Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23) and State Rep. Jamie Flick (R-83) today announced $647,000 has been awarded to two projects in Lycoming and Union counties. The awards were considered at today’s Commonwealth Financing Authority (CFA) meeting and approved through the Authority’s Local Share Account (LSA) statewide program.
“Investing in the equipment students need to train for in-demand careers is an investment in the future of our workforce,” Yaw said. “At the same time, maintaining the infrastructure that serves residents, businesses and major employers is critical to keeping our communities strong. These projects address both needs, and I was pleased to join Rep. Flick in supporting them.”
“I’m pleased to share news of continued support in our district for hands-on training in the high-demand careers of aviation and heavy equipment operation,” said Flick. “Investments in our educational programs and students directly benefit our future workforce and economy. Of equal importance is ensuring our infrastructure is keeping up with growing demand. Both of these projects make good sense, and I am thankful for Sen. Yaw’s valued partnership in projects that strengthen our region.”
Gregg Township Municipal Authority was awarded $400,000 for a sewer line rehabilitation project in Gregg Township, Union County, and Brady Township, Lycoming County. The Authority’s service area spans both townships and serves 233 residential customers, numerous commercial businesses, the Lycoming RMS landfill and the Federal Correctional Complex Allenwood Facility. Funding will be used for the rehabilitation of segments of the sanitary sewer lines, identifying and grading defects to prioritize repairs and cleaning the lines to remove existing blockages.
Lycoming County, on behalf of the Pennsylvania College of Technology, was also awarded $247,000 to purchase equipment for its Aviation and Heavy Equipment Operations degree programs. To support the Aviation program, the College will purchase an AC electric aircraft ground power unit (GPU) and a DC electric aircraft GPU, which will provide necessary power to use avionics training aids for specific learning objectives. To support the Heavy Equipment Operations program, the College will purchase a motor grader with GPS to teach earthmoving and grading.
“Penn College is honored to accept this grant award in support of our aviation and heavy equipment programs, both of which continue to see strong enrollment growth,” said Penn College President Dr. Michael J. Reed. “As technology rapidly evolves across these industries, it is essential that our students learn using the same advanced, industry-standard equipment they will encounter in the workforce. This funding will help us maintain state-of-the-art learning environments and enhance the hands-on educational experiences that prepare graduates for long-term career success.”

title: A Self-Inflicted Wound Pennsylvania Can Still Avoid
raw_text:
A Self-Inflicted Wound Pennsylvania Can Still Avoid
Posted on
September 10, 2026
Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23)
How do you intentionally cut the income of tens of thousands of Pennsylvanians? By undermining an industry that’s become essential to local businesses, veterans’ organizations, fraternal clubs and small businesses across the commonwealth.
For nearly two decades, skill games have been part of Pennsylvania’s local fabric. They help keep neighborhood establishments open, support VFWs and American Legions, fund volunteer fire companies and provide a financial lifeline for organizations and social clubs. In all, thousands of Pennsylvanians rely on the supplemental income from these games, and conservative estimates suggest the industry touches 30,000 to 40,000 livelihoods.
Now, the future of these games is more uncertain than ever. A recent Pennsylvania Supreme Court decision determined skill games fall under the state’s existing gambling laws, declaring the games illegal by October 13 if lawmakers fail to establish a regulatory framework.
At the same time, proposals to address this are being introduced with tax rates so high they could drive skill games out of business entirely. That’s why I introduced Senate Bill 1079 along with Sen. Anthony Williams, which would regulate legitimate skill games, enact a fee-based revenue system, eliminate the bad actors and protect these organizations from devastating taxes they can’t afford.
In 1819, Chief Justice John Marshall wrote “the power to tax is the power to destroy.” Proposed taxation-based models for skill games illustrate this perfectly: high rates that ignore real-world impacts and would crush thousands of jobs and devastate organizations that depend on supplemental income to survive.
If elimination of the industry is the goal, onerous taxation would accomplish it. Businesses will close, jobs will disappear and organizations that rely on them will be left scrambling to make up the difference. The state would also lose the revenue it could have collected from a regulated, viable industry.
But Senate Bill 1079 offers a better path, one that regulates without destroying.
Four years ago, a predecessor to Senate Bill 1079 was ready for action, but legislative delays stalled progress. Those delays have likely cost Pennsylvania about $1 billion in lost revenue. This is money that could have supported services, communities and local needs without raising taxes.
Failing to act now would only deepen that self-inflicted wound.
Skill games aren’t just entertainment. They’re a lifeline. For many Pennsylvanians, they are a paycheck and health benefits. For small businesses, they can mean the difference between keeping the doors open and closing them. For veterans’ organizations, fraternal clubs and volunteer organizations, they provide revenue that helps fund their missions and serve their communities.
Senate Bill 1079 is fundamentally a bill about jobs. It protects the manufacturers who build these machines and the workers who depend on supplemental revenue from them. It supports community organizations, strengthens small businesses and generates significant revenue without burdening ordinary taxpayers.
Pennsylvania has already lost too much. We can’t afford another delay. Senate Bill 1079 deserves immediate action. For the sake of tens of thousands of Pennsylvanians, let’s not make this self-inflicted wound any deeper.
Sen. Gene Yaw was elected to represent the 23rd Senatorial District consisting of Bradford, Lycoming, Sullivan, Tioga and Union counties.

title: Tioga County Awarded State Planning Grant, Lawmakers Say
raw_text:
Tioga County Awarded State Planning Grant, Lawmakers Say
Posted on
September 1, 2026
HARRISBURG – Tioga County has been awarded a $50,000 state grant to update its countywide comprehensive plan, Rep. Clint Owlett (R-Tioga/Bradford) and Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23) announced today.
Tioga County will use the funds to commission the preparation of a county-wide comprehensive plan. Updates to land use mapping, the Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance (SALDO) and zoning language to provide to municipalities will help ensure alignment with land use best practices. The update will also build upon the county’s recently completed housing study by translating the identified needs into implementable land use, zoning and development strategies.
“It is so important for our communities to have big-picture plans in place to guide growth and development while preserving everything we love about living in the Northern Tier,” Owlett said. “I appreciate all the work our county officials put into their planning efforts, and this grant will help them continue that work so our communities are well prepared for what’s ahead.”
“This funding will help Tioga County take a closer look at its housing, development and infrastructure needs and plan for the future,” Yaw said. “A strong comprehensive plan will guide local leaders, support smart decision-making and create opportunities that help keep Tioga County a great place to live and work.”
“We are thankful for the support of Senator Yaw and Representative Owlett in securing this funding for Tioga County,” said Tioga County Commissioners Marc Rice, Sam VanLoon and Shane Nickerson. “This is an important first step in updating our comprehensive plan and taking a thoughtful approach to how our county grows and develops in the years ahead. Through this process, we will work to better understand the priorities of our communities, identify future opportunities and plan for the long-term success of Tioga County. We look forward to working closely with our municipalities and residents to develop a plan that reflects the needs and priorities of Tioga County.”
The funding was awarded through Pennsylvania’s Municipal Assistance Program (MAP), administered by the Department of Community and Economic Development. MAP funding can be used to provide technical assistance to municipalities and other eligible applicants for activities including community planning and implementation.

title: New Research Examines Rural Hospital Sustainability and  Healthcare Market Consolidation in Pennsylvania
raw_text:
New Research Examines Rural Hospital Sustainability and  Healthcare Market Consolidation in Pennsylvania
Posted on
August 19, 2026
Study finds persistent gaps in staffing, services, and health outcomes, with no consistent improvements associated with hospital consolidation
HARRISBURG – Rural hospitals continue to face significant workforce, service, and access challenges, while mergers, acquisitions, and health system affiliations were not associated with consistent improvements across key hospital measures, according to new research released by the Center for Rural Pennsylvania.
The report,
Rural Hospitals in Pennsylvania in the Context of Healthcare Market Consolidations
, was conducted by researchers at The Pennsylvania State University and examines general acute care hospitals across the commonwealth from 2016 through 2023. Researchers combined statewide hospital data with interviews and virtual site visits to examine rural hospital utilization, service availability, quality, financial performance, and changes in hospital ownership.
“Rural hospitals are critical to the health and vitality of the communities they serve,” said Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23), chairman of the Center for Rural Pennsylvania. “This research provides the General Assembly with important Pennsylvania-specific evidence about the challenges these hospitals face and the increasingly complex role of health system partnerships. As we consider the future of rural health care, maintaining access to essential services for rural residents must remain at the center of the conversation.”
The study found that rural hospitals generally operate with fewer physicians and registered nurses, lower patient volumes and occupancy rates, and fewer specialized services than urban hospitals. One of the most pronounced differences involved neonatal care: only about one in five rural hospitals provided Level II or higher neonatal intensive care, compared with approximately one-half of urban hospitals.
Across four major clinical conditions, rural hospitals also had higher mortality rates but lower 30-day readmission rates than urban hospitals, raising questions about how commonly used quality measures should be interpreted in rural settings.
Consolidation Produces a Complex Picture
The study found no consistent improvements in quality, financial performance, staffing, or service availability associated with hospital ownership changes.
Interviews with rural hospital executives and health leaders highlighted both benefits and tradeoffs of health system partnerships. Participants cited greater access to financial resources, specialized services, and administrative support, while also raising concerns about reduced local decision-making and community engagement. The findings suggest that the effects of consolidation depend substantially on the circumstances of individual hospitals and how partnerships are structured and implemented.
“This report underscores that there is no single model for sustaining rural hospitals,” said Zachary L. Adams, Ph.D., executive director of the Center for Rural Pennsylvania. “The evidence points instead to the importance of preserving access to essential services, strengthening the rural healthcare workforce, and ensuring that changes in how care is organized remain responsive to the communities hospitals serve.”
The full report,
Rural Hospitals in Pennsylvania in the Context of Healthcare Market Consolidations
, is available here.
About the Center for Rural Pennsylvania
The Center for Rural Pennsylvania is a bipartisan, bicameral legislative agency of the Pennsylvania General Assembly. Created in 1987 under the Rural Revitalization Act, the Center serves as a resource for rural policy within the General Assembly and works to promote and sustain the vitality of Pennsylvania’s rural and small communities.

title: Yaw, Borowicz: Over $1.2 Million Awarded for Transportation Improvements in Kelly Township
raw_text:
Yaw, Borowicz: Over $1.2 Million Awarded for Transportation Improvements in Kelly Township
Posted on
August 18, 2026
October 6, 2026
HARRISBURG –State Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23) and State Rep. Stephanie Borowicz (R-76) announced $1,210,819 in state funding has been awarded in Kelly Township, Union County though the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation’s (PennDOT) Multimodal Transportation Fund (MTF).
Funding will support Kelly Township’s construction of a new roundabout at Hospital Drive, along with new pedestrian connections to improve accessibility and safety. The project also includes widening and realigning nearby roadways to improve traffic flow and accommodate the new intersection.
“This project is the result of years of advocacy and a lot of hard work and determination by Kelly Township,” Yaw said. “These improvements will make Hospital Drive safer and easier to navigate for residents, hospital patients, employees and emergency responders and I’m pleased to see this important investment in our area finally come to fruition.”
“This $1.2 million is tremendous news for Kelly Township,” said Borowicz. “The new roundabout will improve safety and traffic flow at Hospital Drive and JPM Road while supporting the community’s continued growth.”
The MTF offers funding to improve safety for bicyclists and pedestrians, as well as investments in ports, rail freight and aviation projects. PennDOT selected 50 plans totaling $54 million during this latest application round. Applications for the next round of funding for grants under the MTF will be accepted starting on September 14, 2026.
